power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample was predominantly White (87%) and based in England. During data collection we monitored the political composition of the accruing sample and, observing a skew toward leftleaning participants, introduced party-based quotas. This was not specified in our preregistration. Prolific offers pre-screeners for party affiliation but not left-right orientation. We made this adjustment to better reflect the current UK political landscape. Adjustments were based solely on political demographics and the research team remained blind to responses on all substantive measures throughout. The resulting sample sat just left of centre (M = 2.84, SD = .99). A priori power analyses were conducted using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis calculator for indirect effects (Schoemann et al., 2017), and G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) for the moderation effects. Assuming standardised paths of β = .20, N = 400 provided power of .95 for both parallel indirect effects. For interactions, assuming f² = .02, and power = .80, N = 395 was required, making moderation the binding constraint.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: The Effects Of Misinformation Exposure On Public Attitudes, Prejudice, And The Psychosocial Wellbeing Of Trans And Gender Diverse People: Study 1
table.research_questions:
H1: Greater exposure to TGD-related misinformation will be associated with (H1a) less positive attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people and (H1b) lower support for trans-inclusive policies.
H2: Greater exposure to TGD-related misinformation will be associated with (H2a) greater trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (H2b) higher populist beliefs.
H3: Greater (H3a) trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (H3b) populist beliefs will be associated with less positive attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people and lower support for trans-inclusive policies.
H4: There will be indirect relationships between TGD misinformation exposure and both outcomes (attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people and trans-inclusive policy support), operating through (H4a) trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (H4b) populist beliefs.
H5: Social media information literacy (appraisal) will moderate the relationship between TGD misinformation exposure and (H5a) trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (H5b) populist beliefs, such that the positive associations will be weaker among individuals with higher media literacy.
H6: Parasocial contact with trans and gender diverse people will moderate the relationship between trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (H6a) attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people and (H6b) trans-inclusive policy support, such that the negative associations will be weaker among individuals with greater parasocial contact.
H7: There will be an indirect relationship between TGD misinformation exposure and both outcomes, operating through agreement with the misinformation statements, such that greater exposure will be associated with greater agreement, which in turn will be associated with (H7a) less positive attitudes and (H7b) lower policy support.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Indirect inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to examine a potential causal relationship, but is not designed to isolate the specific causal effect. This work may inform causal inference indirectly or advance insight toward future estimation of a causal relationship.
table.study_design_overview:
Study 1 employs a cross-sectional correlational design using an online self-report survey. The survey will be administered via Qualtrics to participants recruited through Prolific.

Following informed consent, participants will complete the following measures: (1) demographic questions (age, gender, sexual orientation, ethnicity, education, political orientation, religiosity); (2) the TGD Misinformation Exposure Measure (developed in the preliminary phase of this research programme); (3) the TGD Misinformation Agreement Measure (same measure as point two, but measuring agreement), (4) the Trans-Specific Conspiracy Beliefs Scale (Jolley et al., 2025); (5) the Populist Attitudes Scale (Akkerman et al., 2014); (6) the Social Media Information Literacy Appraisal subscale (Heiss et al., 2023); (7) the parasocial TGD contact measure (4 items); (8) the Trans Attitudes and Beliefs Scale (Jones et al., 2023); and (8) the policy support measure (developed in the preliminary phase of this research programme).

Participants will also be asked sporadic attention checks (at least one per measure). This will ask them to "please select [x] for this question". 

Please see the attached open materials document for more information on our exact measures.
table.randomization: The order of the questionnaires and the questions within each questionnaire were randomised across participants.
table.data_collection_procedures:
We will sample 400 self-identifying cisgender people from the United Kingdom (UK) via Prolific. Participants will be paid £12.75/hr for their participation. The purpose of this study is to explore the impact of misinformation exposure around TGD people on cisgender participants from the UK. Study 2 explicitly focuses on the implications of this for TGD participants. 

To ensure that our survey reached the intended sample, we will use the following pre-screeners on Prolific: Cisgender (yes) and Country of Residence (United Kingdom). 

Participants who do not meet our inclusion criteria will be redirected (after answering demographic questions) to a custom end-of-survey message.
table.sample_size_rationale:
A priori power analyses were conducted using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis calculator for indirect effects (Schoemann et al., 2017), and G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) for the moderation effects. For the indirect effects, assuming standardised path coefficients of β = .20, a correlation of r = .30 between the parallel mediators, and 1000 replications with 95% confidence intervals, the analysis indicated that N = 400 provides power of .95 for both the a1b1 and a2b2 indirect effects. This also covers the separate indirect effect proposes in hypothesis seven. 

For the moderation effects, assuming a small interaction effect size (f² = 0.02), alpha = .05 and power = .80, the analysis indicated a required sample size of N = 395. This is, therefore, the binding constraint across all hypotheses. Our target of 400 satisfies both the indirect and moderation power requirements.

Our sample size of 400, therefore, powers this study to detect both the indirect and moderation effects.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop recruiting once we reach 400 participants.
table.measured_variables:
The following variables will be used: 

Trans Attitudes and Beliefs Scale Revised (TABS-R; Jones et al., 2023): This 29-item scale measures attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people. Participants respond on a 7-point scale ranging from (1) strongly disagree to (7) strongly agree. The scale captures three conceptual areas: interpersonal comfort with trans people, beliefs about sex and gender, and recognition of trans people's human value. For example items, see "I would feel comfortable having a trans person into my home for a meal," "A person's gender is determined by what they feel their gender to be and not their sex characteristics," and "Trans individuals are valuable human beings regardless of how I feel about gender identity." This was used as one of our two outcome variables.

Trans-Specific Conspiracy Beliefs Scale (Jolley et al., 2025; Salvati et al., 2023): This 9-item measure is adapted from the Gender Ideology and LGBTQ+ Lobby Conspiracies Scale (Salvati et al., 2023), with the target group changed from "LGBTQ" to "trans people". Items that did not mention a target group in the original scale remain unchanged. The scale captures beliefs about trans people as an organised group seeking power, influence, and societal change. For example items, see "An organised group of trans people works for more power, hiding behind the demand for more rights" and "Trans people want to use laws and courts to impose a precise political view of the world." Participants respond on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) totally disagree to (5) totally agree. This was used as one of our two mediator variables.

Populist Attitudes Scale (Akkerman et al., 2014): This 8-item measure assesses populist ideational beliefs, capturing three theoretical dimensions: anti-elitism, popular sovereignty, and a Manichean worldview. Following prior UK research (Olivas Osuna et al., 2025), the original wording was adapted by replacing "Dutch" with "British" where relevant. Participants respond on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) I very much disagree to (5) I very much agree. For example items, see "The politicians in the British parliament need to follow the will of the people" and "Politics is ultimately a struggle between good and evil." This was used as one of our two mediator variables.

Social Media Information Literacy Appraisal Subscale (Heiss et al., 2023): This 4-item subscale measures participants' self-perceived ability to critically appraise social media information. Participants receive the following instructions: "Thinking about your social media newsfeed and the individual posts or the information you receive on it. How difficult or easy are the following things for you?". Participants indicate their responses on a 7-point scale ranging from (1) difficult to (7) easy. For example items, see "Critically reviewing post content for accuracy" and "Critically examining the credibility of post sources." This was used as one of our two moderator variables.

TGD Parasocial Contact: This 4-item bespoke measure assesses both the frequency and quality of parasocial contact with trans and gender diverse people through media and online platforms. The items were constructed and reviewed by the research team. Frequency items (1 and 2) are answered on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) Never to (5) Frequently, while quality items (3 and 4) are answered on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) Strongly Disagree to (5) Strongly Agree. For example items, see "How often do you watch, follow, or engage with content featuring trans and gender diverse people on social media?" and "When engaging with trans and gender diverse content, I enjoy it." Quality items are only presented to participants who indicated a score of two or more on either of the frequency items. This was used as one of our two moderator variables.

TGD Misinformation Exposure: This bespoke measure assesses the frequency with which participants encounter common forms of TGD-related misinformation in the media and public discussion. The statements were developed and selected through a preliminary ranking survey conducted earlier in this research programme, in which candidate statements were rated for perceived harm and frequency of encounter. Participants rate how often they have encountered each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) never encountered to (5) very frequently encountered. For example items, see "Children under the age of 16 are commonly receiving gender-affirming surgeries" and "Trans women retain unfair physical advantages that make women's sport unsafe or uncompetitive." This was used as our predictor variable.

TGD Misinformation Agreement: Using the same set of statements as the TGD Misinformation Exposure measure, this measure assesses the extent to which participants endorse each claim. Participants indicate how much they agree or disagree with each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) strongly disagree to (5) strongly agree. For example items, see "Children under the age of 16 are commonly receiving gender-affirming surgeries" and "Trans women retain unfair physical advantages that make women's sport unsafe or uncompetitive." This was used as a mediator variable in a confirmatory mediation model estimated separately from the conspiracy-belief and populism mediation (H7). 

TGD Policy Support: This bespoke measure assesses support for trans-inclusive policy positions across four policy issues identified as most prominent in the preliminary ranking survey (single-sex spaces and the Equality Act, participation in competitive sport, access to NHS gender services for under-18s, and prison placement). Each issue is presented as a directional statement keyed toward the trans-inclusive position, and participants indicate their agreement on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) strongly disagree to (5) strongly agree. For example items, see "Trans people should be able to access single-sex spaces and services that align with their gender identity" and "Trans people under 18 should be able to access NHS gender services." Higher scores indicate greater support for trans-inclusive policies. This was used as one of our two outcome variables.

table.statistical_tests:
We will use SEM, conducted with the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) in R (version 4.6.0), to test our hypotheses. All continuous variables will be standardised prior to analysis; reported coefficients will be standardised betas.

Please see the attached model diagram for the proposed paths. Residual covariances will be specified between the two parallel mediators (trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and populist attitudes) and between the two outcomes (trans attitudes and policy support). These covariances acknowledge that the mediators and outcomes are theoretically and empirically interrelated. Covariates (age; political orientation, scored on a left-right scale; and education, entered as a continuous variable) will be entered as predictors of both mediators and both outcomes. Social media information literacy and parasocial TGD contact will be modelled as observed moderator variables.

Interaction terms will be computed by standardising the predictor variable and moderator variable separately and then multiplying them. Specifically:
For H5: standardised TGD misinformation exposure × standardised social media information literacy.
For H6: standardised trans-specific conspiracy beliefs × standardised parasocial TGD contact.
Significant interaction effects will be probed using the Johnson-Neyman technique to identify regions of significance, supplemented by simple slopes analysis at -1 SD, the mean, and +1 SD of the moderator.

We will assess the normality of our data by examining univariate skew and kurtosis. If the data are approximately normal (skew and kurtosis within ±3), we will use the ML estimator. If the data are non-normal, we will use the MLR estimator, which provides robust standard errors and a robust test statistic

Indirect effects (H4a and H4b) will be tested using percentile bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. An indirect effect is considered statistically significant if the 95% confidence interval does not include zero.

The indirect effect of misinformation exposure on both outcomes via agreement (H7) will be tested in a model estimated separately from the conspiracy-belief and populism mediation, using the same approach as above. This separation avoids instability arising from the conceptual overlap between agreement and trans-specific conspiracy beliefs.
Because agreement with anti-trans misinformation and the attitudes outcome are conceptually proximate, we will first report their bivariate correlation as a discriminant-validity check. Should this correlation be very high (r ≥ .80), indicating the two may not be empirically distinct constructs, we will interpret the corresponding mediation with appropriate caution and foreground this limitation. 

Model fit will be assessed using established criteria (Hu & Bentler, 1999): comparative fit index (CFI) ≥ .95, Tucker-Lewis index (TLI) ≥ .95, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) ≤ .06 (with 90% CI upper bound ≤ .08), and standardised root mean square residual (SRMR) ≤ .08.
table.inference_criteria: We will use a probability value of 0.05 when making our inferences. For our indirect effects, we will use the percentile bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (CI). If a CI crosses zero, it is not significant.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude data from participants who do not meet our inclusion criteria, and we will remove any participant who fails two or more of the attention checks into our study. This procedure is consistent with Prolific's policies and is essential to ensuring the high quality of our data.
table.missing_data_handling: Missing data will be handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) under ML estimation.

table.title: The Effects Of Misinformation Exposure On Public Attitudes, Prejudice, And The Psychosocial Wellbeing Of Trans And Gender Diverse People: Study 2
table.research_questions:
H1: Greater exposure to TGD-related misinformation will be associated with (H1a) higher mental distress and (H1b) lower social gender role recognition, controlling for experienced trans-negativity.

H2: TGD community engagement will moderate the relationship between TGD misinformation exposure and (H2a) mental distress and (H2b) social gender role recognition, such that the adverse association between misinformation exposure and each outcome (higher distress, lower recognition) will be weaker at higher levels of community engagement.

H3: TGD community disengagement (attempted disengagement from non-affirming people, communities, and anti-trans content) will moderate the relationship between TGD misinformation exposure and (H3a) mental distress and (H3b) social gender role recognition. Given competing theoretical predictions, the direction of this moderation is not specified.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Indirect inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to examine a potential causal relationship, but is not designed to isolate the specific causal effect. This work may inform causal inference indirectly or advance insight toward future estimation of a causal relationship.
table.study_design_overview:
Study 2 employs a cross-sectional correlational design using an online self-report survey. The survey will be administered via Qualtrics to participants recruited through Prolific.

Following informed consent, participants will complete the following measures: (1) demographic questions (age, region, gender identity, sexual orientation, ethnicity, religion, education, political party, left-right orientation, and transition-related items); (2) the TGD Misinformation Exposure Measure (developed in the preliminary phase of this research programme); (3) the social gender role recognition subscale of the Gender Congruence and Life Satisfaction Scale (GCLS; Jones et al., 2018); (4) the Gender Identity Microaggressions Scale (GIMS; Nadal, 2019); (5) the gender-related discrimination and victimisation subscales of the Gender Minority Stress and Resilience Measure (GMSR; Testa et al., 2015); (6) the Multidimensional Transgender and Nonbinary Resilience Scale (MTNBR; Puckett et al., 2025), from which the Community and Societal Engagement (CSE) and Community and Societal Disengagement (CSD) subscales are used; (7) the GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006); and (8) the PHQ-9 (Kroenke et al., 2001).

Participants will also be asked sporadic attention checks (at least one per measure). This will ask them to "please select [x] for this question". 

Please see the attached open materials document for more information on our exact measures.
table.randomization: The order of the questionnaires and the questions within each questionnaire were randomised across participants.
table.data_collection_procedures:
We will aim to sample 300 TGD people from the United Kingdom (UK) via Prolific. Participants will be paid £12.50/hr for their participation. 

To ensure that our survey reached the intended sample, we will use the following pre-screeners on Prolific: TGD (yes) and Country of Residence (United Kingdom). Participants who do not meet our inclusion criteria will be redirected (after answering demographic questions) to a custom end-of-survey message.

To avoid a sample composed predominantly of one gender group, we will apply a soft quota via Prolific: recruitment will ensure a minimum of 30% binary trans and 30% nonbinary/genderqueer/genderfluid participants, with the remaining 40% unconstrained. No gender-based analyses are planned. This quota concerns sample composition only.
table.sample_size: We will aim to recruit 300 participants.
table.sample_size_rationale:
A priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) for the moderation effects, which represent the binding constraint on sample size in this design. Prior research on community connection as a buffer against minority stress in TGD samples typically reports moderate interaction effects. We therefore powered the study to detect a smallest effect size of interest of f² = 0.035. Assuming alpha = .05 and power = .80, this indicated a required sample size of N = 279. Our target of 300 satisfies this requirement. We note that this design is powered to detect moderate or larger interaction effects; very small interactions may not be reliably detected. 

However, we note that sampling TGD participants in the UK is often challenging and 300 is an ambitious target. Our previous research has demonstrated these issues, with us attaining a sample size less than desired (see: https://doi.org/10.1080/26895269.2025.2483223).
table.stopping_rule: We will stop recruiting once we reach 300 participants or once recruitment stalls. We will stop recruitment short of 300 participants if recruitment fails to yields at least 10 participants over a 7 day period.
table.measured_variables:
The following variables will be used:
TGD Misinformation Exposure: This bespoke measure assesses the frequency with which participants encounter common forms of TGD-related misinformation in the media and public discussion. The statements were developed and selected through a preliminary ranking survey conducted earlier in this research programme, in which candidate statements were rated for perceived harm and frequency of encounter. Participants rate how often they have encountered each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) never encountered to (5) very frequently encountered. For example items, see "Children under the age of 16 are commonly receiving gender-affirming surgeries" and "Trans women retain unfair physical advantages that make women's sport unsafe or uncompetitive." This was used as our predictor variable.

Social Gender Role Recognition (GCLS; Jones et al., 2018): This 4-item subscale of the Gender Congruence and Life Satisfaction Scale assesses the extent to which a person feels their gender is recognised and affirmed by others. Participants respond on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) Never to (5) Always. This was used as one of our two outcome variables.

Gender Minority Stress and Resilience Measure, Gender-Related Victimisation and Discrimination Subscales (GMSR; Testa et al., 2015): Both subscales comprise 11 items (e.g., "Because of my gender identity or expression, I have had difficulty finding a bathroom to use when I am out in public"). 
This 11-item block assesses lifetime experiences of gender identity-related victimisation (6 items) and discrimination (5 items). Participants respond to each item on a four-category scale: Never; Yes, before age 18; Yes, after age 18; Yes, in the past year. For scoring, each item is collapsed to binary (0 = Never, 1 = any endorsement) and summed. This combined score was used as one indicator of experienced trans-negativity (modelled as a latent covariate), alongside the GIMS.

Multidimensional Transgender and Nonbinary Resilience Scale (MTNBR; Puckett et al., 2025): This measure assesses TGD-specific resilience across four subscales. For this study, we use the Community and Societal Engagement (CSE; 8 items) and Community and Societal Disengagement (CSD; 4 items) subscales. Participants respond on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) Strongly Disagree to (5) Strongly Agree. These were used as our two moderator variables. The Individual and Interpersonal subscales were also administered but are not used in the present analyses.

GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006): This 7-item measure assesses symptoms of generalised anxiety over the previous two weeks. Participants respond on a 4-point scale ranging from (0) Not at all to (3) Nearly every day. This was used as an indicator of mental distress (modelled as a latent outcome alongside the PHQ-9).

PHQ-9 (Kroenke et al., 2001): This 9-item measure assesses depressive symptoms over the previous two weeks. Participants respond on a 4-point scale ranging from (0) Not at all to (3) Nearly every day. For an example item, see "Little interest or pleasure in doing things." This was used as an indicator of mental distress (modelled as a latent outcome alongside the GAD-7).

table.indices:
Total scores will be created for each measure. See attached open materials document for the items and scoring metrics used. 

Two constructs are modelled as latent variables in the SEM rather than as observed composites:
Mental distress is modelled as a latent factor with two indicators: total scores on the PHQ-9 (depressive symptoms) and the GAD-7 (anxiety symptoms). Depression and anxiety are highly correlated experiences and combined reflect experiences of mental distress. 

Experienced trans-negativity is modelled as a latent factor with two indicators: sum scores on the Gender Identity Microaggressions Scale and a combined score of the GMSR gender-related discrimination and victimisation items.
table.statistical_tests:
We will use SEM, conducted with the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) in R (version 4.6.0), to test our hypotheses. All continuous variables will be standardised prior to analysis; reported coefficients will be standardised betas.

Please see the attached model diagram for the proposed paths. TGD misinformation exposure will predict two outcomes: mental distress (a latent factor indicated by PHQ-9 and GAD-7 total scores) and social gender role recognition. Experienced trans-negativity (a latent factor indicated by the GIMS and the GMSR victimisation and discrimination subscales) will be entered as a covariate predicting both outcomes. 

A covariance will be freely estimated between TGD misinformation exposure and experienced trans-negativity, and a residual covariance between the two outcomes. Age and experienced transnegativity will be included as covariates in the model. 

We will assess the normality of our data by examining univariate skew and kurtosis. If the data are approximately normal (skew and kurtosis within ±3), we will use the ML estimator. If the data are non-normal, we will use the MLR estimator, which provides robust standard errors and a robust test statistic

Interaction terms will be computed by standardising the predictor variable and moderator variable separately and then multiplying them. Specifically: for H2, standardised TGD misinformation exposure × standardised TGD community engagement; for H3, standardised TGD misinformation exposure × standardised TGD community disengagement. Significant interaction effects will be probed using the Johnson-Neyman technique to identify regions of significance, supplemented by simple slopes analysis at -1 SD, the mean, and +1 SD of the moderator.

Model fit will be assessed using established criteria (Hu & Bentler, 1999): comparative fit index (CFI) ≥ .95, Tucker-Lewis index (TLI) ≥ .95, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) ≤ .06 (with 90% CI upper bound ≤ .08), and standardised root mean square residual (SRMR) ≤ .08.

The TGD misinformation exposure measure was developed using a sample that included TGD participants, and several of the retained statements were rated as very frequently encountered by that group. In the present TGD sample, exposure scores may therefore show some degree of ceiling effect and restricted variance, which could attenuate the predictor's associations with outcomes and reduce power to detect the moderation effects. We will inspect the distribution of exposure scores prior to analysis and report any ceiling effects and their implications for interpretation. Should variance be substantially restricted, this will be considered when interpreting null or weak effects, rather than treated as evidence of no underlying relationship

The code files load 9 distinct packages/libraries: car, dplyr, lavaan, MBESS, plyr, psych, semTools, tidyr, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.
#### Parsable code
All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

-  We found 6 tabular data files and extracted 391 columns from 6 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 2 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata). We ran automated data-quality checks on 391 columns and found no issues. 48 survey respondents were flagged for possible careless responding. We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender.

**What this does not cover.** Only 3 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 4 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:4, File = c("Study 1.Rmd", "Study 2.Rmd", 
"Phase 3.Rmd", "Ranking Survey Analysis Script.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", "numeric", 
"none")), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

text.text: The data from Study 1 and Study 2 were also used to validate the misinformation exposure and policy-support measures reported in a separate paper (Cahill et al., under review).
That paper reports the development and psychometric evaluation of these measures, whereas the present manuscript tests the substantive hypotheses preregistered for each study.
There is no overlap in the hypotheses tested or analyses reported.

Trans and gender diverse (TGD) people, those whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned to them at birth, experience disproportionately high rates of mental health difficulties, including anxiety, depression, and suicidality (Cahill et al., 2026; Jones et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Trans and gender diverse (TGD) people, those whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned to them at birth, experience disproportionately high rates of mental health difficulties, including anxiety, depression, and suicidality <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cahill et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Jones et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Prevalence is substantially higher than among cisgender populations (Hainey et al., 2025), with evidence indicating that these disparities are socially produced rather than reflecting inherent pathology among TGD people (Hoy-Ellis, 2023).
text.formatted: Prevalence is substantially higher than among cisgender populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hainey et al., 2025)</ref>, with evidence indicating that these disparities are socially produced rather than reflecting inherent pathology among TGD people <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hoy-Ellis, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Gender minority stress theory proposes that mental ill-health arises from the cumulative impact of minority stressors (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003), distinguishing distal stressors, such as experiences of discrimination and victimisation, from proximal stressors, such as expectations of rejection, identity concealment, and internalised stigma.
text.formatted: Gender minority stress theory proposes that mental ill-health arises from the cumulative impact of minority stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hendricks & Testa, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Meyer, 2003)</ref>, distinguishing distal stressors, such as experiences of discrimination and victimisation, from proximal stressors, such as expectations of rejection, identity concealment, and internalised stigma.

text.text: The attitudes and behaviours of cisgender people are, therefore, an active social determinant of minority stress, and are shaped by a public information environment that is increasingly negative towards TGD people (Bracco et al., 2024; Connolly et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The attitudes and behaviours of cisgender people are, therefore, an active social determinant of minority stress, and are shaped by a public information environment that is increasingly negative towards TGD people <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bracco et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Connolly et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Tan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Negative discourses surrounding TGD people are especially acute in the United Kingdom (UK), where the legal, political and social position of TGD people has shifted markedly.

Since 2025, the UK has fallen below the European average for LGBTQ+ rights protections, ranking 22 nd of 49 countries in the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map (ILGA-Europe, 2025).
text.formatted: Since 2025, the UK has fallen below the European average for LGBTQ+ rights protections, ranking 22 nd of 49 countries in the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(ILGA-Europe, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This decline has coincided with highly publicised developments affecting the rights and social position of TGD people, including the UK Supreme Court ruling in 2025 on the essentialist definition of sex under the Equality Act 2010, subsequent Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance published in 2026, and publication of the Cass Review in 2024.

These developments have intensified debate about trans rights, within an information environment where anti-TGD claims circulate widely and often unchallenged, alongside a broader rise in populist and conspiratorial politics across Europe and North America.
Central to this environment is misinformation, defined here as false or misleading information that spreads, regardless of intent to deceive (Meade et al., 2024; The Alan Turing Institute, 2024).
text.formatted: Central to this environment is misinformation, defined here as false or misleading information that spreads, regardless of intent to deceive <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Meade et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">The Alan Turing Institute, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Misinformation is distinguished from simple error by being repeated, shared, and frequently politically motivated, accruing credibility through familiarity rather than evidence (Ludwig & Sommer, 2024).
text.formatted: Misinformation is distinguished from simple error by being repeated, shared, and frequently politically motivated, accruing credibility through familiarity rather than evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Ludwig & Sommer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Anti-TGD misinformation frequently travels alongside two related belief systems: populism, a worldview pitting a virtuous ordinary people against a self-serving corrupt elite (Akkerman et al., 2014; Olivas Osuna et al., 2025), and conspiracy beliefs which attribute events to the secret, malevolent coordination of powerful groups (Jolley et al., 2025; van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018).
text.formatted: Anti-TGD misinformation frequently travels alongside two related belief systems: populism, a worldview pitting a virtuous ordinary people against a self-serving corrupt elite <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Akkerman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Olivas Osuna et al., 2025)</ref>, and conspiracy beliefs which attribute events to the secret, malevolent coordination of powerful groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jolley et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These constructs are mutually reinforcing: populist and conspiratorial worldviews render misinformation more credible, and exposure to misinformation, particularly through social media, strengthens conspiratorial thinking (Chan et al., 2026; Enders et al., 2023).
text.formatted: These constructs are mutually reinforcing: populist and conspiratorial worldviews render misinformation more credible, and exposure to misinformation, particularly through social media, strengthens conspiratorial thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chan et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Enders et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In the TGD context, this coalesces in narratives casting trans people and their allies as an organised "gender ideology" lobby pursuing hidden influence (Salvati et al., 2024, p. 301).
text.formatted: In the TGD context, this coalesces in narratives casting trans people and their allies as an organised "gender ideology" lobby pursuing hidden influence <ref type="bibr">(Salvati et al., 2024, p. 301)</ref>.

text.text: Both belief systems are associated with more hostile intergroup attitudes and reduced support for minority-protective policy, although the evidence is considerably stronger for conspiracy beliefs.

Conspiracy beliefs about sexual and gender minorities predict prejudice and opposition to LGBTQ+ rights (Jolley et al., 2025; Salvati et al., 2024), and perceived minoritygroup status shapes which conspiratorial claims gain traction (Gundersen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Conspiracy beliefs about sexual and gender minorities predict prejudice and opposition to LGBTQ+ rights <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jolley et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Salvati et al., 2024)</ref>, and perceived minoritygroup status shapes which conspiratorial claims gain traction <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gundersen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Such narratives may be especially potent because they recast a minority seeking rights as a coordinated threat to the majority, licensing hostility while presenting it as self-defence (Ching, 2022; Jolley et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such narratives may be especially potent because they recast a minority seeking rights as a coordinated threat to the majority, licensing hostility while presenting it as self-defence <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Ching, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Jolley et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These narratives have long been leveraged against LGBTQ+ people, such as during the AIDS crisis, where conspiracy theories about gay men proliferated (Heller, 2015).
text.formatted: These narratives have long been leveraged against LGBTQ+ people, such as during the AIDS crisis, where conspiracy theories about gay men proliferated <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Heller, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Populism's contribution is less certain.

It may supply the people versus elite scaffolding onto which anti-TGD claims are hung (Paternotte & Kuhar, 2018), and populist attitudes are linked to exclusionary orientations toward outgroups (Olivas Osuna et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It may supply the people versus elite scaffolding onto which anti-TGD claims are hung <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Paternotte & Kuhar, 2018)</ref>, and populist attitudes are linked to exclusionary orientations toward outgroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Olivas Osuna et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, only some forms of populism are associated with negative outgroup attitudes (Akkerman et al., 2017; Olivas Osuna et al., 2025), and populist antagonism is directed primarily upwards, at elites (Rooduijn et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, only some forms of populism are associated with negative outgroup attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Akkerman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Olivas Osuna et al., 2025)</ref>, and populist antagonism is directed primarily upwards, at elites <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Rooduijn et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Whether populist beliefs are associated with prejudice towards TGD people therefore warrants scrutiny.

Within the UK, these belief systems attach to defined policy flashpoints, including single-sex spaces, competitive sport, NHS gender services to under-18s, and prison placement, where public attitudes are strongly shaped by gender-related beliefs (Connolly et al., 2025; Flores et al., 2016 Flores et al., , 2020).
text.formatted: Within the UK, these belief systems attach to defined policy flashpoints, including single-sex spaces, competitive sport, NHS gender services to under-18s, and prison placement, where public attitudes are strongly shaped by gender-related beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Connolly et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Flores et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Flores et al., , 2020</ref>).

text.text: Yet direct evidence linking exposure to anti-TGD misinformation with prejudice and policy attitudes remains scarce, particularly within the UK. Connolly and colleagues (2025) position pervasive social and press media misinformation as a central driver of an increasingly hostile UK environment for TGD people.
text.formatted: Yet direct evidence linking exposure to anti-TGD misinformation with prejudice and policy attitudes remains scarce, particularly within the UK. <ref type="bibr">Connolly and colleagues (2025)</ref> position pervasive social and press media misinformation as a central driver of an increasingly hostile UK environment for TGD people.

text.text: However, this link has been argued at the level of review rather than tested, individual-level relationships between misinformation exposure, prejudice, policy attitudes, and wellbeing unexamined.
A further question concerns whether exposure translates into belief.
Encountering a claim is not the same as accepting it, and repeated exposure may breed acceptance through familiarity or, for some, invite scepticism (Ludwig & Sommer, 2024).
text.formatted: Encountering a claim is not the same as accepting it, and repeated exposure may breed acceptance through familiarity or, for some, invite scepticism <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Ludwig & Sommer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because misinformation exposure has typically been inferred from broader belief systems rather than measured against the specific claims in circulation, whether agreement with those claims accounts for the link between exposure and attitudes remains untested.
These associations are unlikely to be uniform across cisgender individuals.
Social media information literacy, the capacity to critically appraise online content, may weaken the link between exposure and belief (Heiss et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Social media information literacy, the capacity to critically appraise online content, may weaken the link between exposure and belief <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Heiss et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Parasocial contact, the one-sided sense of connection formed with TGD media figures, extends the prejudice-reducing benefits of intergroup contact (Schiappa et al., 2005) and improves attitudes towards TGD people specifically (Chen & Zhang, 2022; Massey et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Parasocial contact, the one-sided sense of connection formed with TGD media figures, extends the prejudice-reducing benefits of intergroup contact <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Schiappa et al., 2005)</ref> and improves attitudes towards TGD people specifically <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chen & Zhang, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Massey et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Miller et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Across two experiments, Jolley et al. (2025) demonstrated that cisgender people's positive parasocial contact with TGD creators on TikTok did not directly reduce trans conspiracy beliefs, but increased perspective-taking, which was in turn associated with lower conspiracy beliefs.
text.formatted: Across two experiments, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Jolley et al. (2025)</ref> demonstrated that cisgender people's positive parasocial contact with TGD creators on TikTok did not directly reduce trans conspiracy beliefs, but increased perspective-taking, which was in turn associated with lower conspiracy beliefs.

text.text: In data pooled across three studies, more frequent positive contact with trans people showed the same indirect pathway. Jolley et al. (2025) found that parasocial contact with TGD creators reduced trans conspiracy beliefs indirectly, via perspective-taking, and note that such beliefs are related to, but distinct from, prejudice.
text.formatted: In data pooled across three studies, more frequent positive contact with trans people showed the same indirect pathway. <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Jolley et al. (2025)</ref> found that parasocial contact with TGD creators reduced trans conspiracy beliefs indirectly, via perspective-taking, and note that such beliefs are related to, but distinct from, prejudice.

text.text: Parasocial contact may therefore do more than lower conspiracy beliefs.
Among those who hold them, familiarity with individual TGD people may weaken the extent to which beliefs about a coordinated trans lobby translate into negative evaluations and policy opposition.
TGD people are also directly affected by this information environment.

Within gender minority stress theory, a public discourse saturated with hostile and inaccurate claims can be understood as a distal stressor in its own right, becoming a chronic, ambient signal of societal rejection that need not take the form of a discrete interpersonal event to be harmful (Hendricks & Testa, 2012).
text.formatted: Within gender minority stress theory, a public discourse saturated with hostile and inaccurate claims can be understood as a distal stressor in its own right, becoming a chronic, ambient signal of societal rejection that need not take the form of a discrete interpersonal event to be harmful <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hendricks & Testa, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike interpersonal discrimination, which is episodic, a hostile media climate is continuous and difficult to escape, reaching even those who are otherwise insulated from face-to-face prejudice (Meyer, 2003; Pang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Unlike interpersonal discrimination, which is episodic, a hostile media climate is continuous and difficult to escape, reaching even those who are otherwise insulated from face-to-face prejudice <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Meyer, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Pang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This exposure may bear on two facets of TGD wellbeing in particular: mental health and the sense of being recognised in one's gender.
Frequent encounters with anti-TGD misinformation may, therefore, be associated with poorer mental health, including heightened anxiety and depression (Wall et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Frequent encounters with anti-TGD misinformation may, therefore, be associated with poorer mental health, including heightened anxiety and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wall et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Further, exposure to negative TGD media has been associated with reduced access to gender affirming care in Sweden (Indremo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Further, exposure to negative TGD media has been associated with reduced access to gender affirming care in Sweden <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Indremo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such exposure may also erode social gender-role recognition, the sense that one's gender is recognised and affirmed by others (Jones et al., under review), an aspect of gender congruence closely tied to wellbeing (Jones, Bowe, et al., 2023; Jones et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Such exposure may also erode social gender-role recognition, the sense that one's gender is recognised and affirmed by others <ref type="bibr">(Jones et al., under review)</ref>, an aspect of gender congruence closely tied to wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Jones, Bowe, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Jones et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This is because public questioning of whether trans identities are legitimate targets precisely the external affirmation on which recognition depends.
Coping with these harms is often buffered by social connectedness with others who share similar lived experiences (Frost & Meyer, 2012; Jones et al., 2026; Puckett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Coping with these harms is often buffered by social connectedness with others who share similar lived experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Frost & Meyer, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Jones et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Puckett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In response to stigma and exclusion, TGD people may withdraw from social groups and environments perceived as unsafe.
While such withdrawal can protect against immediate harm, it may also limit access to social support.
For example, TGD young people who distance themselves from unsupportive family frequently report unmet emotional and practical support needs (Jones et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, TGD young people who distance themselves from unsupportive family frequently report unmet emotional and practical support needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Jones et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, avoiding hostile physical activity environments can reduce opportunities for social connection, identity affirmation, and wellbeing (Jones et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Similarly, avoiding hostile physical activity environments can reduce opportunities for social connection, identity affirmation, and wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Jones et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, connections with other TGD and LGBTQ+ people can foster belonging, social support, and collective efficacy, promoting resilience (Jones et al., 2026).
text.formatted: By contrast, connections with other TGD and LGBTQ+ people can foster belonging, social support, and collective efficacy, promoting resilience <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Jones et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Disengagement from TGD community spaces, including online spaces where hostile content circulates may therefore be double-edged, reducing exposure to harmful content while limiting opportunities for connection and collective support.
Research on misinformation and on gender minority stress has developed largely in parallel.
The first has examined how misinformation, conspiracy beliefs and populism shape intergroup attitudes and policy preferences (Jolley et al., 2025; Olivas Osuna et al., 2025; Salvati et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The first has examined how misinformation, conspiracy beliefs and populism shape intergroup attitudes and policy preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jolley et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Olivas Osuna et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Salvati et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The second has examined how hostile social environments affect the wellbeing of minoritised groups (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003; Puckett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The second has examined how hostile social environments affect the wellbeing of minoritised groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hendricks & Testa, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Meyer, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Puckett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, no research has examined anti-TGD misinformation among cisgender and TGD people concurrently, nor has UK research measured exposure to the specific claims currently in circulation, as distinct from endorsement of broader conspiracy or gender-ideology beliefs.

The present research addresses both pathways across two concurrent quantitative studies, advancing a dual-pathway account in which anti-TGD misinformation may harm TGD communities indirectly, by degrading the surrounding attitudinal climate, and directly, by acting as a minority stressor.

Both studies draw on a set of contemporary, UK-specific misinformation and policy-support measures developed for this programme through community-engaged focus groups and a ranking survey (Cahill et al., under review).
text.formatted: Both studies draw on a set of contemporary, UK-specific misinformation and policy-support measures developed for this programme through community-engaged focus groups and a ranking survey <ref type="bibr">(Cahill et al., under review)</ref>.

text.text: Study 1 assesses whether cisgender people's exposure to anti-TGD misinformation is associated with less positive attitudes towards TGD people and lower support for transinclusive policiesfoot_0 , whether these associations operate through conspiracy beliefs and populist attitudes, whether agreement with the misinformation statements accounts for these associations, and whether they are moderated by social media information literacy and parasocial contact.
text.formatted: Study 1 assesses whether cisgender people's exposure to anti-TGD misinformation is associated with less positive attitudes towards TGD people and lower support for transinclusive policies<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> , whether these associations operate through conspiracy beliefs and populist attitudes, whether agreement with the misinformation statements accounts for these associations, and whether they are moderated by social media information literacy and parasocial contact.

text.text: Study 1 hypotheses are as follows:  H1: Greater anti-TGD misinformation exposure will be associated with (a) less positive attitudes and (b) lower policy support.

 H2: These associations will be mediated by (a) trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (b) populist attitudes, such that greater exposure will be associated with stronger beliefs, which will in turn be associated with less positive attitudes and lower policy support.

 H3: Social media information literacy will moderate the association between anti-TGD misinformation exposure and (a) trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (b) populist attitudes, such that the positive associations will be weaker among those with higher literacy.

 H4: Parasocial contact with TGD people will moderate the association between transspecific conspiracy beliefs and (a) attitudes and (b) policy support, such that the negative associations will be weaker among those with greater parasocial contact.

 H5: Anti-TGD misinformation exposure will be indirectly associated with (a) less positive attitudes and (b) lower policy support via agreement with the misinformation statements, tested in a model estimated separately from H2.

Study 2 turns to TGD people, examining whether misinformation exposure functions as a minority stressor associated with greater mental distress and reduced social gender-role recognition, and whether TGD community engagement and disengagement moderate these relationships.

We control for participants' experiences of trans-negativity (gender-based discrimination, victimisation and microaggressions), to test whether misinformation exposure is associated with these outcomes over and above them.

We make the following hypotheses for Study 2:  H1: Greater anti-TGD misinformation exposure will be associated with (a) higher mental distress and (b) lower social gender-role recognition, controlling for experienced trans-negativity.

 H2: TGD community engagement will moderate these associations, such that the adverse association between misinformation exposure and (a) mental distress and (b) social gender-role recognition will be weaker at higher levels of engagement.
 H3: TGD community disengagement will moderate these associations.
Given competing theoretical predictions, we do not specify a direction.
Method Study 1's design, sampling procedure, hypotheses and analysis plan were preregistered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MRQ4H).

text.text: We employed an online cross-sectional survey hosted on Qualtrics and recruited via Prolific.
Our final sample comprised 400 participants who self-identified as cisgender people from the UK, aged 18 to 75 (M age = 39.2, SD age = 12.6).
Table 1 displays the sample composition.

text.text: The sample was predominantly White (87%) and based in England.
During data collection we monitored the political composition of the accruing sample and, observing a skew toward leftleaning participants, introduced party-based quotas.
This was not specified in our preregistration.
Prolific offers pre-screeners for party affiliation but not left-right orientation.
We made this adjustment to better reflect the current UK political landscape.
Adjustments were based solely on political demographics and the research team remained blind to responses on all substantive measures throughout.
The resulting sample sat just left of centre (M = 2.84, SD = .99).
A priori power analyses were conducted using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis calculator for indirect effects (Schoemann et al., 2017), and G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) for the moderation effects.

text.text: Assuming standardised paths of β = .20, N = 400 provided power of .95 for both parallel indirect effects.
For interactions, assuming f² = .02, and power = .80, N = 395 was required, making moderation the binding constraint.
Nottingham Trent University's Research Ethics Committee granted ethical clearance.
Propagating the very misinformation we sought to study posed a clear ethical risk.
To mitigate this, participants in both studies were presented at debrief with a corrective document that directly refuted each misinformation statement used (see the OSF).

TGD Parasocial Contact: was measured with a bespoke 4-item measure of the frequency (e.g., "how often do you watch, follow, or engage with content featuring trans and gender diverse people on social media?") and quality (e.g., "when engaging with trans and gender diverse content, I enjoy it") of contact through media and online platforms, each rated from 1 to 5.
The two quality items were shown only to participants scoring two or more on either frequency item, so the six participants reporting no contact were scored on the frequency items alone.
Higher mean scores indicated greater TGD parasocial contact.

text.text: Higher scores indicate greater support for trans-inclusive policies.
This was used as one of our two outcome variables.
All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.6.0).
All continuous predictor, mediator, moderator, and outcome variables were standardised prior to analysis, and reported coefficients are standardised betas.
We tested our hypotheses using structural equation modelling in the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012).

text.text: Residual covariances were estimated between the two mediators and between the two outcomes.
Models were estimated using maximum likelihood, with full information maximum likelihood (FIML) used to handle missing data so that all available data were retained.

Indirect effects were tested using the product-of-coefficients approach, with percentile 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals based on 5000 resamples; an indirect effect was considered present where the confidence interval did not contain zero (Yzerbyt et al., 2018).

text.text: The moderating roles of social media information literacy and parasocial TGD contact were tested via standardised interaction terms.
We controlled for age (in years), political orientation (left-right), and education (as a continuous variable).
For transparency, the pattern of findings was unchanged with and without these covariates.
We additionally tested an indirect effect of misinformation exposure via agreement with the misinformation statements in a separately estimated model.
Because agreement with antitrans misinformation and the attitudes outcome are conceptually proximate, we first examined their bivariate correlation as a discriminant-validity check.

We pre-specified that a very high correlation (r ≥ .80) would indicate that the two may not be empirically distinct constructs, in which case we would interpret the corresponding mediation with appropriate caution and foreground this limitation.
Given the potential correlation between the predictor variables, moderator and mediator variables, we assessed and determined that the variance inflation factor was acceptable (VIF < 2).

text.text: The TABS showed excellent reliability, as did the Trans-Specific Conspiracy Beliefs Scale and the Social Media Information Literacy appraisal subscale.
The Populist Attitudes Scale was the weakest performer, though still acceptable.

Encouragingly, the bespoke measures developed for this research cohered well: misinformation exposure, misinformation agreement, policy support, and parasocial contact all demonstrated good internal consistency.
Descriptively, participants reported relatively positive attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people but below the midpoint support for trans-inclusive policies.
Reported exposure to and agreement with misinformation were both around the scale midpoint, as was parasocial contact.
Conspiracy beliefs were comparatively low, while populist attitudes sat above the midpoint.

text.text: Agreement with misinformation was very strongly associated with both attitudes (r = -.82) and policy support (r = -.78) and was closely linked to conspiracy beliefs (r = .81).

Given the strong correlations between agreement and the outcome variable (attitudes), and the fact it shows strong conceptual overlap with conspiracy theories, this additional analysis should be interpreted with caution.
We first assessed the model fit against our pre-registered criteria (CFI ≥ .95, TLI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .06, with 90% CI upper bound ≤ .08, and SRMR ≤ .08).
Two indices indicated excellent fit (CFI = .98; SRMR = .02) and two fell short of our pre-registered cutoffs (TLI = .90; RMSEA = .08, 90% CI [.06, .11]).
The TLI fell only marginally short, and the RMSEA is known to over-reject correctly specified models at low degrees of freedom, as here (df = 10; Kenny et al., 2015).

text.text: The SRMR, which is not subject to this penalty, indicated excellent fit, as did the standardised residuals (all ≤ .06, bar one at -.16).
Most modification indices suggested atheoretical reverse paths.
The exception, and the source of the largest residual, was the unmodelled association between parasocial contact and conspiracy beliefs.

We did not add this path, as contact was pre-registered as a moderator of the mediator-outcome paths rather than as a predictor of the mediators, and adding it would have been a data-driven departure from the pre-registered model.
As such, we deemed the model to appropriately represent the data.

text.text: The following results relate to our pre-registered hypotheses.

Misinformation exposure was significantly and positively associated with both proposed mediators: conspiracy beliefs, β = .22, 95% CI [.14, .31], p < .001, and populist attitudes, β = .15, 95% CI [.05, .24], p = .002.

text.text: Conspiracy beliefs were, in turn, significantly and negatively associated with both attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people, β = -.45, 95% CI [-.54, -.35], p < .001, and policy support, β = -.28, 95% CI [-.38, -.18], p < .001.
text.formatted: Conspiracy beliefs were, in turn, significantly and negatively associated with both attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people, β = -.45, 95% CI [-.54, -.35], p < .001, and policy support, β = -.28, 95% CI [-.38, -.18], p < .001.

text.text: Populist attitudes, however, predicted neither attitudes, β = -.03, 95% CI [-.10, .05], p = .484, nor policy support, β = .04, 95% CI [-.04, .11], p = .333.

Consistent with this pattern, the indirect effect of misinformation exposure through conspiracy beliefs was significant for both attitudes, β = -.10, 95% CI [-.15, -.06], and policy support, β = -.06, 95% CI [-.10, -.03].
The indirect effects through populist attitudes were nonsignificant for both outcomes (attitudes β = -.004, 95% CI [-.02, .01]; policy β = .005, 95% CI [-.01, .02]).

Regarding the direct effects, misinformation exposure was not significantly associated with attitudes in the full model, β = -.04, 95% CI [-.10, .03], p = .247, but was significantly, if modestly, associated with policy support, β = -.08, 95% CI [-.15, -.002], p = .042.

When looking at the bivariate relationships between misinformation exposure and each outcome while only controlling for the covariates, there was a significant relationship with both outcomes (attitudes β = -.12, 95% CI [-.20, -.04], p = .003; policy β = -.11, 95% CI [-.19, -.03], p = .006).
The relationship between exposure and both outcomes therefore operated substantially through conspiracy beliefs rather than populist attitudes.
Neither of the pre-registered moderation hypotheses was supported.

The misinformation exposure by media literacy interaction was not significantly associated with conspiracy beliefs, β = -.03, 95% CI [-.10, .05], p = .433, or populist attitudes, β = .03, 95% CI [-.06, .13], p = .523.

Similarly, the conspiracy beliefs by parasocial contact interaction was not associated with attitudes, β = .04, 95% CI [-.03, .11], p = .248, or policy support, β = -.05, 95% CI [-.14, .04], p = .347, and the populism by parasocial contact interaction was also nonsignificant for both outcomes (attitudes β = -.04, p = .349; policy β = -.003, p = .933).

text.text: Media literacy, parasocial contact, their interaction terms, and the covariates (age, education, political orientation) were included in the model but are omitted for clarity; all interaction effects were non-significant (see text).

Study 1 examined whether cisgender people's exposure to anti-TGD misinformation was associated with attitudes towards TGD people and support for trans-inclusive policies, and whether these associations operated through conspiracy beliefs and populist attitudes.
Greater misinformation exposure was associated with stronger conspiracy beliefs and stronger populist attitudes.
However, only conspiracy beliefs were associated with more negative attitudes and lower policy support.
The indirect effects through conspiracy beliefs were significant for both outcomes, while those through populist attitudes were not.
In an additional analysis, agreement with the misinformation statements fully accounted for the association between exposure and both outcomes.
Neither social media information literacy nor parasocial contact moderated the hypothesised pathways.
However, parasocial contact was directly associated with more positive attitudes and greater policy support.
A key finding was that the direct associations between exposure and the two outcomes (attitudes towards TGD people and policy support) were largely explained by the mediators.

The direct association with attitudes became non-significant, and the direct association with policy support remained significant but small, the latter suggesting exposure may also shape policy preferences through routes not captured here.
Importantly, this was driven entirely by conspiracy beliefs, with no indirect association through populist attitudes for either outcome.
This difference between the two mediators may partly reflect how the two constructs were measured.
The Trans-Specific Conspiracy Beliefs Scale frames TGD people as an organised group pursuing hidden influence, whereas the Populist Attitudes Scale makes no reference to TGD people.

Conceptually, conspiracy beliefs also tend to be directed at specific groups (van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018), whereas populist attitudes are directed primarily at elites and may not reliably extend to hostility towards outgroups (Rooduijn et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Conceptually, conspiracy beliefs also tend to be directed at specific groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018)</ref>, whereas populist attitudes are directed primarily at elites and may not reliably extend to hostility towards outgroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Rooduijn et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This is consistent with the weaker evidence base for populism noted earlier and suggests populism may reflect a general antagonistic framing rather than one directed at TGD people specifically.
Encountering TGD misinformation was not, in itself, strongly related to TGD attitudes.
Instead, acceptance of those claims was central, such that agreement with the misinformation statements accounted for the association between exposure and both outcomes.

This is consistent with the illusory truth effect, whereby repeated exposure to a claim increases its perceived credibility (Fazio et al., 2015; Hasher et al., 1977), and with evidence linking frequent exposure to misinformation to greater belief (e.g., Udry & Barber, 2023).
text.formatted: This is consistent with the illusory truth effect, whereby repeated exposure to a claim increases its perceived credibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fazio et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hasher et al., 1977)</ref>, and with evidence linking frequent exposure to misinformation to greater belief (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Udry & Barber, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It is therefore acceptance of the claims, rather than the encounter itself, that appears to matter for how people evaluate TGD people (Ludwig & Sommer, 2024).

text.text: However, agreement correlated at -.82 with attitudes and .81 with conspiracy beliefs, and whether it represents a distinct construct or a further indicator of a single evaluative orientation remains unclear.
The same may apply to the conspiracy beliefs measure itself, which could partly capture this broader orientation rather than a separate set of beliefs.
Neither moderation hypothesis was supported.

Media literacy has been proposed as a protective resource against misinformation (Guess et al., 2018 (Guess et al., , 2020) ) with interventions reliably improving people's ability to distinguish accurate from inaccurate information; however, their effects on subsequent attitudes are smaller and less consistent (Droog et al., 2026).

text.text: As media literacy was self-reported here, the null finding may partly reflect a gap between perceived and actual ability to identify misinformation.

Alternatively, participants better able to recognise misinformation may have been no less likely to hold the beliefs it supports, particularly where those beliefs aligned with existing political commitments (Van Bavel et al., 2024).

text.text: Parasocial contact showed a substantial direct association with both outcomes but did not buffer the path from conspiracy beliefs to either outcome.
We had reasoned that familiarity with individual TGD people might weaken the extent to which conspiracy beliefs translate into negative evaluations.

However, Jolley et al. (2025) found that parasocial contact with TGD creators did not directly reduce conspiracy beliefs, but increased perspective-taking, which was in turn associated with lower conspiracy beliefs.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Jolley et al. (2025)</ref> found that parasocial contact with TGD creators did not directly reduce conspiracy beliefs, but increased perspective-taking, which was in turn associated with lower conspiracy beliefs.

text.text: This positions contact as operating on those beliefs rather than on their consequences.
Our results are broadly consistent with that account.
Contact was also associated with lower conspiracy beliefs in the present sample (r = -.41), consistent with the pooled association reported by Jolley and colleagues.
As perspective-taking was not measured here, whether it accounts for the association between parasocial contact and the outcomes remains a question for future research.
However, given the cross-sectional design, it is equally plausible that people with more positive attitudes towards TGD people are more likely to seek out TGD creators in the first place.

Our final sample comprised 290 participants who self-identified as trans or gender diverse from the UK, who were aged 18 to 58 (M age = 28.1, SD age = 7.7).

The order of the measures and the order of the items within each measure were randomised.

We made two wording changes for affirming language and UK relevance: "gender reassignment" became "gender transition", and the reference to the DMV became "at the hospital or GP".
Our analysis approach followed Study 1, with two differences.

First, two constructs were modelled as latent factors rather than observed composites: mental distress, indicated by PHQ-9 and GAD-7 total scores, and experienced trans-negativity, indicated by GIMS total scores and a combined GMSR discrimination and victimisation score.

Because the loadings of each two-indicator factor were constrained to unity, we report unstandardised coefficients as the primary estimates, alongside fully standardised coefficients for comparability.

Second, the pre-registration specified a covariance between misinformation exposure and trans-negativity and a residual covariance between the two outcomes but did not address covariances between trans-negativity and the remaining exogenous variables.
We therefore allowed trans-negativity to covary with all other exogenous variables.
Age and experienced trans-negativity were included as covariates.

text.text: We also assessed univariate normality, which we deemed acceptable as skew and kurtosis were all within ±2.
Descriptively, misinformation exposure scores fell slightly above the scale midpoint (M = 3.65, SD = .89; possible range 1-5).
Mean scores on both mental health measures exceeded the clinical thresholds for depressive symptoms (M = 11.14, SD = 6.57) and for anxiety symptoms (M = 9.22, SD = 5.61).
In total, 57.2% of participants scored at or above the threshold for clinically relevant depressive symptoms and 57.9% for clinically relevant anxiety symptoms.

text.text: In this table, we include the composite of the latent factors for trans-negativity (comprised of microaggressions and overt discrimination and victimisation) and mental distress (comprised of PHQ-9 and GAD-7) that are used in the subsequent primary models, rather than the individual scales themselves.
Internal consistency was generally good to excellent across each of the measures used.
However, internal consistency for community disengagement was poorer.
As such, any coefficients relating to community disengagement, including the interaction term, should be interpreted cautiously.

The pre-registered model, in which the loadings of both two-indicator latent factors were freely estimated, fitted the data poorly (CFI = .92, TLI = .85, RMSEA = .08, 90% CI [.06, .10], SRMR = .07) and produced a large number of inadmissible bootstrap solutions (1,703 of 5,000), reflecting the instability of latent factors with only two indicators.
We therefore made two changes.
First, we constrained the loadings within each latent factor to equality (i.e., both fixed to 1), a common approach to stabilising two-indicator factors.
Second, we allowed the latent trans-negativity factor to covary with all other predictors in the model (community engagement and disengagement, their interaction terms, and age).
The findings from both models remained consistent.
Model fit was assessed against the same pre-registered criteria as Study 1 and showed the same pattern.
CFI (.97) and SRMR (.03) indicated excellent fit, while TLI (.91) and RMSEA (.07, 90% CI [.04, .09]) fell below our cutoffs.
As in Study 1, the two shortfalls were on indices sensitive to model size and parsimony, whereas the SRMR, which carries no such penalty, indicated excellent fit.

Standardised residuals were all ≤ .07 except two involving social gender-role recognition, and the modification indices suggested only a pair of equal and opposite residual covariances between the trans-negativity indicators and social gender-role recognition, for which we had no theoretical justification.
We therefore retained the model (see Figure 2).
