text.text: The following results relate to our pre-registered hypotheses.

Consistent with H1a, greater exposure to TGD-related misinformation was significantly and positively associated with mental distress, b = 0.13, 95% CI [0.02, 0.24], β = .14, p = .024, controlling for experienced trans-negativity.
H1b was not supported: exposure was not significantly associated with social gender role recognition, b = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.09], β = -.02, p = .689.
Neither of the pre-registered moderation hypotheses was supported.

Contrary to H2, the misinformation exposure by community engagement interaction was not significantly associated with mental distress, b = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.11], p = .803, or with social gender role recognition, b = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.04], p = .162.

Similarly, and with no direction specified a priori, the exposure by community disengagement interaction was not significantly associated with mental distress, b = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.17, 0.03], p = .175, nor with social gender role recognition, b = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.21], p = .091.
Neither community engagement nor community disengagement therefore buffered or amplified the association between misinformation exposure and either outcome.
The following observations were not pre-registered and are reported as exploratory.
Community engagement was associated with lower mental distress, b = -.13, 95% CI [-.26, -.02], β = -.15, p = .035.

Community disengagement was associated with greater social gender role recognition, b = .21, 95% CI [.08, .34], β = .21, p = .002, though given its lower internal consistency this should be interpreted cautiously.

Experienced trans-negativity was strongly associated with both greater mental distress, b = .58, 95% CI [.39, .80], β = .48, p < .001, and lower social gender role recognition, b = -.38, 95% CI [-.64, -.16], β = -.28, p = .002.

Study 2 examined whether exposure to anti-TGD misinformation was associated with mental distress and reduced social gender-role recognition for TGD people themselves, and whether community engagement or disengagement moderated these associations.
Greater misinformation exposure was associated with higher mental distress but was unrelated to social gender-role recognition.
Experienced trans-negativity, by contrast, was associated with lower social gender-role recognition.
Neither community engagement nor disengagement moderated these associations.
Levels of mental distress were high, with 57.2% and 57.9% of participants scoring above the clinical thresholds for depressive and anxiety symptoms, respectively (i.e., PHQ-9 ≥ 10; GAD-7 ≥ 8).

The association between misinformation exposure and mental distress remained significant when experiences of discrimination, victimisation and microaggressions were controlled for, suggesting that anti-TGD misinformation may represent an aspect of minority stress not fully accounted for by experienced trans-negativity.
This is consistent with treating a hostile information environment as a distal stressor, rather than as a proxy for interpersonal mistreatment (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: This is consistent with treating a hostile information environment as a distal stressor, rather than as a proxy for interpersonal mistreatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hendricks & Testa, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Unexpectedly, anti-TGD misinformation exposure was unrelated to social gender-role recognition, which we anticipated would be particularly vulnerable to public questioning of the legitimacy of TGD identities (Jones et al., under review).
text.formatted: Unexpectedly, anti-TGD misinformation exposure was unrelated to social gender-role recognition, which we anticipated would be particularly vulnerable to public questioning of the legitimacy of TGD identities <ref type="bibr">(Jones et al., under review)</ref>.

text.text: Whether a person's gender is recognised by others may relate more to interpersonal relationships or transition-related circumstances than to national discourse.
This may explain why trans-negativity, which is encountered interpersonally, was associated with lower social gender-role recognition, whereas misinformation exposure was not.

If so, environmental stressors of this kind may bear on generalised distress while leaving identity-specific appraisals relatively untouched, a distinction worth pursuing in future minority stress research.
Neither moderation hypothesis was supported.
The absence of buffering by community engagement is surprising, given consistent benefits of community connectedness for TGD wellbeing (Frost & Meyer, 2012; Puckett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The absence of buffering by community engagement is surprising, given consistent benefits of community connectedness for TGD wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Frost & Meyer, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Puckett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, while these direct benefits are well established (Mezza et al., 2024; Valentine & Shipherd, 2018), evidence that connection buffers the effects of minority stressors is less consistent (Mezza et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, while these direct benefits are well established <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mezza et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Valentine & Shipherd, 2018)</ref>, evidence that connection buffers the effects of minority stressors is less consistent <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mezza et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings mirror this pattern as engagement was directly associated with lower distress, but it did not buffer the association between misinformation exposure and distress.
That said, the present study may have been underpowered to identify modest buffering effects.
A further possibility concerns how community engagement relates to the stressor itself.
Minority stress theory proposes that community resources attenuate stress by allowing members to reappraise stigma collectively as a feature of society rather than of themselves (Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: Minority stress theory proposes that community resources attenuate stress by allowing members to reappraise stigma collectively as a feature of society rather than of themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This may be less effective when the community is also a route through which the stressor is encountered.

Interpersonal discrimination is experienced individually and can be met with collective support, whereas a hostile information climate reaches the whole community, so those to whom TGD individuals turn face the same stressors (Wall et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Interpersonal discrimination is experienced individually and can be met with collective support, whereas a hostile information climate reaches the whole community, so those to whom TGD individuals turn face the same stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wall et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, exposure was positively associated with engagement in our sample, perhaps because community spaces also circulate, discuss and contest anti-TGD content.
Where engagement involves repeated discussion of hostile claims, it may itself become a stressor (Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: Where engagement involves repeated discussion of hostile claims, it may itself become a stressor <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This does not in itself explain the absence of an interaction, but suggests that engagement may operate as a channel of exposure as well as a source of support.
Exposure was also positively associated with disengagement, consistent with disengagement being a response to hostile content rather than simply the opposite of engagement.
This distinction has implications for how the buffering hypothesis is specified.
Minority stress theory does not generally distinguish between community resources as sources of support and as sources of exposure.
Our findings suggest that this distinction may matter (see also Cahill et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Our findings suggest that this distinction may matter (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Cahill et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Community connection demonstrates consistent benefits (Mezza et al., 2024; Valentine & Shipherd, 2018), but may have little purchase on a stressor that reaches the community through the same networks that provide support.
text.formatted: Community connection demonstrates consistent benefits <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mezza et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Valentine & Shipherd, 2018)</ref>, but may have little purchase on a stressor that reaches the community through the same networks that provide support.

text.text: The disengagement findings warrant caution.
Internal consistency for this subscale was poor (ω = .65), so the null interactions may reflect a genuine absence of moderation or attenuation due to measurement error.
In exploratory analyses, disengagement was directly associated with greater social gender-role recognition, but not with distress.
Whether withdrawal from a hostile discourse shields TGD people or isolates them remains open, and addressing it will require a more reliable measure.
Importantly, only 16.2% of the Study 2 sample were trans women, despite trans women being the principal subject of anti-trans narratives in the UK (Bracco et al., 2024; Connolly et al., 2025).

text.text: Three of the four policy areas identified through our item development, single-sex spaces, participation in competitive sport and prison placement, are most often associated with trans women (Connolly et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2017).

text.text: This may nonetheless limit generalisability, as experiences of minority stress could vary across gender groups with trans women experiencing higher levels of some forms of trans-negativity (Evje et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This may nonetheless limit generalisability, as experiences of minority stress could vary across gender groups with trans women experiencing higher levels of some forms of trans-negativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Evje et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should deliberately oversample trans women, and, where sample size permits, examine whether these associations differ across TGD identities given minority stress exposure is not evenly distributed (Hainey et al., 2025; Rimes et al., 2019).

text.text: Across two concurrent studies, we examined whether exposure to anti-TGD misinformation that specifically relates to TGD people was associated with cisgender people's attitudes towards TGD people and support for trans-inclusive policies (Study 1), and whether it was associated with mental distress and social gender role recognition for TGD people themselves (in Study 2).

Among cisgender participants, greater exposure was associated with less positive attitudes and lower support for trans-inclusive policies, and these associations operated largely through trans-specific conspiracy beliefs rather than through populist attitudes.

Among TGD participants, greater exposure was associated with higher mental distress, over and above experiences of gender-based discrimination, victimisation and microaggressions, though it was not associated with social gender-role recognition.
Both arms of the dual pathway we proposed therefore received some support, albeit asymmetrically.

The direct association between misinformation exposure and both outcomes in Study 1 was largely explained by conspiracy beliefs and, in a separate model, by agreement with the misinformation statements once those variables were accounted for.
In Study 2, misinformation exposure was associated with mental distress after controlling for trans-negativity.
The same information environment may, therefore, operate through two distinct mechanisms depending on people's identities.
For cisgender people it functions persuasively, with harm arising through what is believed; for TGD people it functions as an ambient stressor, with harm arising through what is encountered.
This is consistent with evidence that restrictive anti-TGD legislation is associated with poorer mental health among TGD people irrespective of individual endorsement (Lee et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is consistent with evidence that restrictive anti-TGD legislation is associated with poorer mental health among TGD people irrespective of individual endorsement <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lee et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As such, interventions addressing the two are unlikely to be the same.

Established approaches to countering misinformation, including debunking and fact-checking, psychological inoculation or prebunking, accuracy prompts, and media literacy training, all operate primarily on how information is received and evaluated (Droog et al., 2026; Kozyreva et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Established approaches to countering misinformation, including debunking and fact-checking, psychological inoculation or prebunking, accuracy prompts, and media literacy training, all operate primarily on how information is received and evaluated <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Droog et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Kozyreva et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Each targets the pathway identified in Study 1 and based on our findings such approaches may be well placed to protect the attitudinal climate surrounding TGD people.
None of them, however, reduces the volume of TGD misinformation content in circulation, which is the feature of the environment that Study 2 suggests matters for TGD people themselves.
Protecting TGD wellbeing would, therefore, require either changes to the information environment itself or forms of support that help people live within an environment that is unlikely to change.

This is a demanding prospect given evidence that anti-TGD misinformation is increasing (Billard, 2023 (Billard, , 2024;; Connolly et al., 2025) and recent changes by key social media companies that have loosened content moderation, including of hateful content (e.g., Paul et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is a demanding prospect given evidence that anti-TGD misinformation is increasing <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Billard, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Billard, , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Connolly et al., 2025)</ref> and recent changes by key social media companies that have loosened content moderation, including of hateful content (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Paul et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: It also identifies a gap in that the intervention literature is largely organised around belief, while one of the two harms we document does not run through belief at all but rather simple exposure.

A further observation spanning both studies was the absence of moderation: neither social media information literacy nor parasocial contact moderated the hypothesised associations in Study 1, and neither community engagement nor disengagement moderated either association in Study 2.
For community engagement in particular, this replicates our previous findings.
In a national sample of 5856 TGD young people in the UK, access to

LGBTQ+ affirming spaces and perceived community acceptance were consistently and independently associated with better mental health, yet showed no evidence of buffering gender minority stressors (Cahill et al., 2026).
text.formatted: LGBTQ+ affirming spaces and perceived community acceptance were consistently and independently associated with better mental health, yet showed no evidence of buffering gender minority stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cahill et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: That study attributed the null partly to the reduced variability of binary moderator indicators, but the present study used continuous measures and reached the same conclusion.

Taken together, these findings suggest that community-level resources may operate additively rather than conditionally, contrary to one of the central predictions of minority stress theory (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: Taken together, these findings suggest that community-level resources may operate additively rather than conditionally, contrary to one of the central predictions of minority stress theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hendricks & Testa, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: We would not read this as evidence that buffering does not occur.

Interaction effects demand considerably more power than main effects, cross-sectional designs are poorly suited to capturing processes that unfold over time, and our study examined only two of many possible community resources.

What our findings do suggest is that the additive benefits of affirming environments should not be assumed to extend to conditional protection against a hostile public discourse, and that buffering hypotheses may need to be specified with reference to the kind of stressor involved.
The role of political orientation also warrants comment.
It was the strongest single association in the Study 1 model, exceeding that of misinformation exposure itself, and our Study 2 sample was predominantly left-leaning.
It is therefore difficult to establish how far misinformation exposure operates independently of prior ideological commitments.

Participants already holding more conservative positions may encounter, attend to and accept these claims more readily, consistent with accounts of politically motivated reasoning (Van Bavel et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Participants already holding more conservative positions may encounter, attend to and accept these claims more readily, consistent with accounts of politically motivated reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Van Bavel et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our design prevents us from distinguishing between these possibilities, and we advise against interpreting our findings as evidence that exposure exerts influence independently of the political commitments that shape it.
Several limitations should be considered.
Most importantly, both studies were crosssectional, and the direction of the associations we report cannot be established.
It is equally plausible that participants holding more negative attitudes towards TGD people sought out, attended to and recalled more TGD-related misinformation.
The very strong association between agreement with the misinformation statements and attitudes is consistent with this limitation.
In Study 2, participants experiencing greater distress may have been more vigilant towards, or more likely to recall, hostile content.
Cross-sectional designs are also poorly suited to detecting buffering, since such effects may reflect processes unfolding over time (Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: Cross-sectional designs are also poorly suited to detecting buffering, since such effects may reflect processes unfolding over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Several measurement limitations also apply.
Exposure was self-reported, and recognition of a claim may be inflated by familiarity with it, particularly among those who already agree with it.
Study 2 also did not measure proximal processes, such as appraisals of the misinformation encountered or expectations of rejection, through which exposure may be associated with distress.

In addition to the poor internal consistency for the community disengagement subscale, the misinformation items developed for this project were intended to capture claims circulating in the UK at the time of data collection (2026) and are, by design, time limited.
Our sample was also predominantly White and based in England which limits the generalisability of the findings.
Future research should use longitudinal or diary designs to establish the temporal ordering of exposure, distress and community engagement, as these would also be better placed to detect buffering.
A broader range of potential moderators should also be examined.

Among cisgender samples, experimental designs manipulating exposure could establish whether exposure shapes conspiracy beliefs and attitudes, and, given the direct associations observed for parasocial contact in Study 1, contact-based interventions warrant evaluation alongside belief-focused approaches.
In conclusion, anti-TGD misinformation was associated with harm along two pathways.

Among cisgender people, exposure was associated with less positive attitudes towards TGD people and lower support for trans-inclusive policies, largely through acceptance of the claims themselves, particularly when those claims were conspiratorial.
Among TGD people, exposure was associated with greater mental distress, consistent with misinformation acting as a minority stressor.
None of the protective factors we examined weakened either pathway, although parasocial contact with TGD people was beneficial in its own right.

Tackling the first pathway is likely to need interventions that address both belief and contact, whereas tackling the second will mean attending to the information environment itself and to how TGD people can be supported within it.
